After cleaning by heating andfor alternating fields 87 per cent yielded directions with agS < lo", comprising 435 dykes, 12 sills and one granite; polarities could be determined for some of the remainder. Directions are thought to be primary and on average are shallower than corresponds to the mean centred axial dipole, with many shallow reversely-magnetized dykes present. Seventeen per cent of the dykes are normally magnetized, 5 per cent have intermediate directions. Polarity does not correlate with petrography, thick- ness or trend, but does depend upon location. In particular, on the NE coast up to 70 per cent are normal, and possibly belong to a different swarm. Normal polarities were found for both sites in the Northern Granite, for Holy Island and for some of the sills. In conjunction with the known stra- tigraphy this shows that the rocks were formed during an R-N-R sequence of polarities, or more probably R-N-R-N. Within the S Arran swarm, Knaap bands c, d and e show a greater NW trend than the rest. Superficially these distributions of trend together with the distribution of polarities noted above suggest a link between polarity and trend particularly in the northeast of the island. However, closer examination does not confirm this. Although in the present study dyke trends were not measured in the field, it is possible to read some approximate values from the aerial photographs. The histograms of Fig. 5 display the results for bands 6 and 7 and show that there is no clear correlation of polarity with trend. It would appear that the correlation is with location rather than trend. Knaap has suggested that some of the dykes in NE Arran may belong to the NW Arran dyke swarm and the Bute sub-swarm rather than the main S Arran swarm. The predominant trend of the NW Arran swarm is between 300-310" (although there is a wide spread from 270 to 060') and that of the Bute sub-swarm 50-100". The latter directions are present in band 6 but with no preferred polarity, while for band 7 the former trend is represented only by normal dykes

On the basis of the experience reported by Lovlie, Lowrie & Jacobs (1971), we would expect this separation to be fairly efficient for spinel-type iron oxides (magnetite and maghemite) but very inefficient for hematite, hydrated iron oxides, or paramagnetic minerals. X-ray diffraction patterns of these separates showed definitely that the principal mineral was a spinel-type oxide, and a line at 3.75A implied the presence of maghemite. Microscopic examination of polished sections of this material confirmed the predominance of maghemite and revealed ubiquitous exsolution lamellae within the maghemite grains. We did investigate one sand sample from the late Pleistocene Kibish Formation (de Heinzelin et al. 1970), which un- conformably overlies the Shungura Formation and is thought to have a similar source area. The magnetic separate from the Kibish Formation was also dominated by exsolved maghemite, but in addition contained a small amount of magnetite. This datum suggests the hypothesis that the destruction of magnetite occurred in part after deposition of the Shungura and Usno Formations. We performed stepwise thermal demagnetization at 50°C increments in air on a few whole samples using a Schoenstedt TSD-1 oven (heating field 150 gamma, cooling field 10 gamma). The directional measurements from the 600-650°C range were close to the directional measurements from the 200-600°C range, regardless of orientation of the sample in the oven. In addition, the intensity remaining at 600°C was surprisingly high, about 10 per cent of the initial intensity. The directional measurements from the 600-650°C range were close to the directional measurements from the 200-600°C range, regardless of orientation of the sample in the oven. The most likely explanation of this observation is that some of the NRM is due to hematite which is magnetized in the same direction as any other components. From these data it is clear that we are not dealing with simple detrital magnetite but rather with oxidized sediments in which maghemite and hematite are contributing to remanence. For late Cenozoic red sediments in Baja, California, Larson & Walker (1975) reported that different component minerals (hematite, geothite, and 'hydropsilomelane') had different polarities so that where several components were present the net magnetiza- tion was in an intermediate direction (i.e. neither normal nor reversed). We do not have the same situation because for most samples a moderate partial demagnetization results in clear normal or reverse polarity and further demagnetization does not generally change the direction. One sample of variety (a) was collected from the surface level. 3.4 WESSELTON MINE, 10 KM SEE OF KIMBERLEY Wesselton is one of the five major kimberlite pipes in the immediate vicinity of Kimberley. The kimberlites intrude rocks of the Karroo System, which overlies lavas of the Ventersdorp System with intervening quartzite horizons. According to Allsopp & Barrett (1975), the radiometric age of the Wesselton Pipe is 84 f 3 Myr. The surface area of the pipe is 10 x lo4,*. The rocks occupying the pipe can be divided into three groups based on textural and petrographical characteristics. Group 1 contains all non-fragmental varieties of kimberlite, Group 2 is intrusive breccias containing variable amounts of xenolithic material and Group 3 is volcanic breccias having an agglomeratic or tuffaceous appearance. of continents and oceans in Late Precambrian and Early Palaeozoic is one of the key problems in Earth sciences and is now the subject of debate. Palaeomagnetic data when combined with geological criteria, with faunal distributions and with palaeo- climatic indicators may indicate the generation and destruction of former oceans. However, for the Late Precambrian and Early Palaeozoic times the accuracy and the distribution of control points on apparent polar wandering curves prevent unequivocal solutions (McElhinny & Embleton 1976). In this paper we present the palaeomagnetic data and the isotopic age from a sequence of igneous rocks (Alcaparrosa Formation) in western Argentina assigned to the Late Ordovician. We also compare the reliable palaeomagnetic poles for South America assigned to the Late Ordovician (this paper), Cambrian (Thompson 1973) and Late Precambrian (Vilas & Pacca 1978), with results from the rest of Gondwana. Palaeomagnetic data from 71 hand samples of igneous rocks of Late Ordovician age exposed in western Argentina (31.3"S, 69.4" W, Alcaparrosa Formation) are given. Stable remanent magnetization was isolated in the majority of samples; they yield a palaeomagnetic pole at 56"s 33"E (N= 8, = 16"). Whole rock K-Ar age determinations yield an age of 416 5 10 Myr for a pillow lava of the Alcaparrosa Formation. Palaeomagnetic data for South America, Africa, Australia, Antarctica and India suggest that Gondwana was a unit at least as far back as 1000 Myr. The palaeomagnetic data define a rapid polar migration for Gondwana in Ordo- vician time which is consistent with the widespread occurrences of Late Ordovician glacial deposits across this supercontinent. In order to contribute to the resolution of the problem of the plate tectonic character of the Caribbean, a palaeomagnetic study has been carried out on some Jamaican igneous rocks. Sixteen Late Cretaceous intru- sives and lavas and one Late Miocene lava sampled in five sites have been investigated. Because of widespread maghaemitization of the predominantly large-grained deuteric class 1 titanomagnetites, some difficulty was experienced in identifying stable directions of magnetization in the Creta- ceous rock units. Using thermal demagnetization technique, two distinct directions of magnetization were obtained, significantly different from those observed in contemporaneous North American rocks. Nine units yield a palaeomagnetic pole at 143.8OW, 44.1°N, referred to as 'normal', while seven units yield 'equatorial' poles situated both east and west of Jamaica. It is not possible to decide which of the two directions of magnetization reflects the Late Cretaceous geomagnetic field in Jamaica, but from other evidence they appear to merit palaeotectonic interpretation. Introduction During the summers of 1970 and 1973 a total of 34 volcanic flows from four separate loca- tions in the Absaroka Mountains of northwest Wyoming were sampled for a paleomagnetic study. The primary objective of this program was to establish paleomagnetic criteria with which to correlate sequences of flows belonging to the Absaroka Volcanic Supergroup [Smedes and Prostka, 1972]. These flows were extruded in the Eocene Epoch [Nelson and Pierce, 1968; Smedes and Pro- stka, ]972], a time when the earth's field was reversing frequently [Heirtzler et al., 1968]. Both normal and reversed polarities are present in the sampled flows, thus providing an excellent basis for correlation. The grain sizes and compositions of the primary magnetic phases, their thermomagnetic characteristics as reflecting high- temperature oxidation, and properties of secondary magnetic phases were studied in an attempt to identify the sources of stable and unstable magnetism in the Yellowstone tuffs. Per- tinent observations are discussed in t, he following sections. Grain Size of Magnetic Minerals Magnetite and titanomagnetite grains range in size from about 400 to less than I urn. Grains of very fine particle size (less than 2 urn) are ubiquitous (Figure 6), and they probably carry most of the stable remanence observed in the three tuffs [see Ozima and Ozima, 1965; Verhoogen, 1959; Larson et al., 1969]. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: igan 48109 The paleomagnetism of 103 samples from purplish gray sandstones of the Juniata Formation has been investigated. The samples were collected at 17 sites in Virginia, West Virginia, and Pennsylvania. Thermal demagnetization showed a strong magnetic overprinting in a large number of samples. This magnetization is secondary, since it was acquired during or after the late Paleozoic folding of the area; the resulting pole position, at 47øN, 129øE, agrees with published Late Carboniferous to Early Permian pole positions for North America. In all but 12 samples, directions of another component of magnetization could be determined in thermal demagnetization up to 672øC. These are assumed to represent the original magnetization of the Juniata Formation; they were acquired before the folding, and they show both normal and reversed polarities. The resulting pole position, at 31.5øN, 114,4øE (k = 55, a95 = 5ø), falls directly in between published Middle Ordovician and Late Silurian pole positions for cratonic North America. It is, of course, possible that the magnet- ization revealed after limited treatment is the initial, perhaps because it is the only one carried by the rock. However, because the experimental work was not sufficient to ascertain whether another magnetization was present or not, the result remains uncertain and controversial. Therefore we believe that a minimum of laboratory experiments should be performed on all rock units. For igneous and metamorphic rocks, both extensive af and thermal treatments are necessary; af alone is inadequate to identify the remanence carriers (e.g., magnetite or hematite). Thermal and chemical remanent magnetization are often found to coexist in such rocks, and either of them could be of initial or secondary origin. Thermal cleaning will at least pro- vide one with the TB of the different carriers, and it might then be possible to establish the origin and sequence of magnet- ization [Buchan and Dunlop, 1976; Roy and Lapointe, 1976]. A detailed study (nine sites: mean pole at 190øE, 16øS) of a 5.3-m stratigraphic section at Jacobsville shows significant apparent polar motion and the occurrence of at least one field reversal. The trend of the pole movement relative to North America was then southward. Vector analyses show that during the acquisition of the intermediate and late phase remanences the apparent pole started to move northward; by the end of the magnetization process it had reached high latitude (307øE, 72øN). Explanation of the Jacobsville results and other high-latitude poles requires a major revision of the apparent polar path during the Hadrynian. The proposed path executes a loop into the southern hemisphere (- l100 to -950 m.y.) and then roughly follows a great circle path (Hadrynian Track) from 160øE near the equator up to the present north geographic pole and down to the equator at 340øE (-670 m.y.). Much of the mountainous terrain of the Lassiter Coast region consists of highly folded Upper Jurassic argillaceous sandstone and silt- stone (Latady Formation) and overlying or laterally equiva- lent silicic to intermediate volcanic rocks which have been interpreted as being deposits of a Mesozoic arc system [Suarez, 1976]. The Latady and volcanic rocks were strongly folded around north to northeast striking axes sometime between Late Jurassic and Late Cretaceous time. The Jurassic sequence was intruded, partially refolded, and contact-metamorphosed by Upper Cretaceous plutons of diorite to granite composition [Williams and Rowley, 1971; Williams et al., 1972; Rowley, 1973; Kellogg and Rowley, 1974; Plummet, 1974; Rowley and Williams, 1974]. Eight published K-Ar age determinations obtained from plutonic rocks of the southern and central Lassiter Coast range from 119 m.y. to 95 m.y. [Mehnert et al., 1975; Rowley et al., 1975]. Eight other K-Ar age determina- tions from plutonic rocks of the northern Lassiter coast and southern Black Coast exhibit a similar range in age [Rowley et al., 1976]. Owing to the high latitude of the Antarctic Peninsula since at least the mid-Jurassic, reconstructions such as these are open to question unless, specifically, the uncertainty in declination is considered; such considerations were not made in these previous studies. Paleomagnetic data from the entire length of the Antarctic Peninsula [Blurtdell, 1962; Dalziel et al., 1973; Scharnberger, 1974, and unpublished data, 1974; Kellogg and Reynolds, 1974; Reynolds and Kellogg, 1974] are now sufficiently abun- dant to test the theories of oroclinal bending. This paper reports paleomagnetic results from the Lassiter Coast and defines confidence limits on mean declinations from all avail- able data from the Antarctic Peninsula in order to test the hypothetical models of structural bending. INTRODUCTION The Devonian paleomagnetic field for North America is not well known; there are few published data, and those that are available show considerable scatter. Consequently, the posi- tion of North America with respect to the earth's rotation axis and to the other continents lacks adequate definition for paleo- geographic reconstructions and plate tectonic analysis in the mid-Paleozoic. Until recently, results considered to be representative of the Devonian of North America came from paleomagnetic studies chiefly of lavas and red beds of the Upper Devonian Perry Formation of Maine and New Brunswick [Black, 1964; Phil- lips and Heroy, 1966; Robertson et al., 1968]. However, a recent investigation of Lower to Middle Devonian limestones from Ohio [Marti n, 1975] gave a paleomagnetic pole near to the late Paleozoic pole position for North America and some 15 ø away from the mean Perry pole. It is difficult to attribute the differ- ence in the pole position to a particular cause, such as appar- ent polar wander with respect to North America in the Devon- ian, without additional data. This report describes a paleomagnetic study of reddish silt- stones and sandstones within the Middle to Upper Devonian Ca

nd red beds of the Upper Devonian Perry Formation of Maine and New Brunswick [Black, 1964; Phil- lips and Heroy, 1966; Robertson et al., 1968]. However, a recent investigation of Lower to Middle Devonian limestones from Ohio [Marti n, 1975] gave a paleomagnetic pole near to the late Paleozoic pole position for North America and some 15 ø away from the mean Perry pole. It is difficult to attribute the differ- ence in the pole position to a particular cause, such as appar- ent polar wander with respect to North America in the Devon- ian, without additional data. This report describes a paleomagnetic study of reddish silt- stones and sandstones within the Middle to Upper Devonian Catskill deposits of New York. The results of this study enable us to propose a resolution to the apparent discrepancy in North American Devonian palcomagnetic data on the basis of paleogeography and to discuss the relevance of these and other late Paleozoic paleomagnetic data to the formation of the Euramerican supercontinent. In total, 107 samples were measured and demagnetized. The natural remanent magnetization of the samples was measured with Schonstedt, cryogenic and Digico magnetometers. This pole position trend of about 25’ matches very well the North American appar- ent polar wander path between Early Permian and Early Triassic. It could be argued that this “agreement” results in a conflict between the apparent magnetic age (Permian) and the Early to Late Triassic age generally assigned to the Chugwater Group. However, similar progressions of paleomagnetic pole positions have been reported for the Early Triassic Moenkopi Formation in Colorado; thus it appears that long-term variations and swings characterized the geomagnetic field at that time. With detailed paleomagnetic sampling, these features can be utilized for stratigraphic correlation in addition to magnetic-reversal stratigraphy. This will eliminate, to some degree, part of the non-uniqueness inherently present in correlations based on reversal stratigraphy only. The type section is the large cliffs southwest of the village of Maubisse in the Central highlands of East Timor (see Figs. 1 and 2). Here the Formation consists of well-bedded dense limestone and massive reefs. Chocolate red, dark and grey green shales occur as thin developments within the limestone. Near Mt. Ramelau there occurs a sequence of strongly coloured metamorphosed basic volcanics. Outside the type section the Maubisse Formation is fairly widespread forming distinctive features in the landscape. Audley-Charles (1968) regards the Maubisse as allochthonous and inter- prets the field relations to indicate that it rests tectonically on the autoch- thonous Aitutu (Triassic) and Wai Luli (Jurassic) Formation. The limestones produced a rich fauna, which suggests an age ranging from Early to Late Permian (Audley-Charles, 1968). ity of Africa, contains within its borders a considerable variety of rocks and geological structures. The rela- tionship of the Hercynian belt to the West African (Saharan) craton may be determined, and this may then be compared to sequences known primarily from southern Africa. ity of Africa, contains within its borders a considerable variety of rocks and geological structures. The rela- tionship of the Hercynian belt to the West African (Saharan) craton may be determined, and this may then be compared to sequences known primarily from southern Africa. ity of Africa, contains within its borders a considerable variety of rocks and geological structures. The rela- tionship of the Hercynian belt to the West African (Saharan) craton may be determined, and this may then be compared to sequences known primarily from southern Africa. More recently very careful studies of these redbeds have shown (Wensink, 1968, 1975; Klootwijk, 1973, 1974b, 1975b) that it is necessary to carry out detailed thermal demagnetization to high tempera- tures because of the presence of a persistent secondary magnetization of apparent Early Tertiary age. These authors have associated this overprint with the extrusion of the Deccan Traps extensively over the Peninsular Shield region. It is not at all clear how such widespread remagnetization of the sediments could result from the extrusion of thick lava piles except very close to the lava contact. Klootwijk (1975b, 1976) suggested the remag- netization resulted from the acquisition of a viscous partial th~rmorem~ence due to sustained heating at temperatures between 100” and 200°C while the traps were being extruded o

and 200°C while the traps were being extruded over a prolonged period. This effect coupled with chemical remagnetization resulting from the associated hydrothermal effects is regarded as the source of the hard secondary magnetization. Whatever the cause, the presence of this hard secondary component in sediments from the Peninsular Shield has cast considerable doubt on the validity of some of the earlier studies. Part of the problem has arisen because of the general lack of availability of sensitive magnetometers capable of measuring the very small primary compo- nent that is still preserved after thermal dema~etizat~on close to the Curie Temperature. In this paper we report further results from the Bhander and Rewa Series of the Vindhyan System that confirms the extensive presence of a hard secondary component of apparent Early Tertiary age. We also report the first palaeomagnetic measurements from the Permo-Carboniferous Panjal Traps of Kashmir. Until this time the rather curious fact that these volcanics are extremely weakly magnetized has prevented investigators in India from carrying out any palaeomagnetic studies of them (R.K. Verma and R.N. Athavale, personal communication). SAMPLING AND MEASUREMENTS The samples investigated in this study were collected durin

the neighbouring Hari Parbat Hill. A single flow was collected in a road cutting in the Wular Lake region where the traps are directly overlain by Triassic limestone. The samples were originally measured on a PAR SMl Spinner Magnetom- eter but the surprisingly weak intensities observed in the Panjal Traps neces- sitated putting these aside until they could be processed using a Digico Com- plete Results Magnetometer. Although some of the initial measurements on all the collections were made on the SMl ~a~etometer the final analyses and cleaned measurements were made on the Digico Magnetometer. Alter- nating field demagnetization and thermal demagnetization procedures were carried out on apparatus described by McElhinny (1966) and McElhinny et al. (1970), respectively. However, the mean pole position for these rocks lies at 32N 2823 and this is almost identical with that observed in the Deccan Traps (Wensink, 1973). Whatever the cause, the presence of this hard secondary component in sediments from the Peninsular Shield has cast considerable doubt on the validity of some of the earlier studies. Volcanic conglomerate, as much as 70 m in aggregate thickness, locally constitutes the basal Nikolai. Most of the basalt erupted subaerially, but at a few localities in the McCarthy quadrangle some near-basal flows are pillowed, indicating sub- aqueous extrusion. Nikolai basalts weather to medium brown or, less commonly, greenish, yellowish, or reddish brown. They are mainly porphyritic and contain medium-grained plagio- clase or augite phenocrysts in a fine-grained inter- granular groundmass comprising plagioclase, augite, opaque minerals, minor relict olivine, sphene, and apatite. The secondary minerals include abundant chlorite along with hydrous iron oxides, epidote, calcite, sericite, clay minerals, prehnite, quartz, ferruginous ser- pentine minerals, pumpellyite, and rare zeolites. Many of these minerals occupy veinlets or amygdules. Although the alteration effects are widespread, they are rarely intense or pervasive enough to obliterate primary minerals and textures; consequently, the name 'green- stone' is a misnomer for the Nikolai basalts. The secondary mineral assemblages indicate widespread deuteric alteration and local prehn- ite-pumpellyite facies

Many of the larger magnetite grains contain intergrowths of titanohematite and possibly sphene in fine lamellae apparently controlled by the crystal structure of the parent grains. This lamellar texture is commonly observed in fresh subaerial basalts and is believed to be due to high- temperature oxidation of primary titanomagne- tite during cooling of the magma (Buddington and Lindsley 1964). However, the lamellae ob- i served in fresh basalts typically consist of ilmenite rather than titanohematite or sphene. In the Nikolai basalts the replacement of ilmenite by sphene is probably the result of chemical alteration during burial metamorphism. Sphene lamellae associated with magnetite have been observed in prehnite-pumpellyite facies meta- basalts of the Karmutsen Formation on Van- couver Island, where the replacement of ilmenite was attributed to burial metamorphism (Kuni- yoshi and Liou 1976). Assuming certain physical conditions (pressure, chemical compositions, etc.), Kuniyoshi and Liou estimated that prehn- ite-pumpellyite metamorphism of the Kar- mutsen basalts occurred at temperatures between 250°C and 350°C. [Traduit par le journal] Introduction and adamellitic rocks which range from diorite Paleomagnetic studies of Precambrian rocks from North America carried out during the past 15 years, and especially during the past 5 years, have allowed reasonable estimates to be made of the path of polar wander during much of Proterozoic time. This path is the signature of Precambrian continental drift. Although there is plenty of scope for differences of opinion on details, it is now clear that the path consists of a number of loops which may be thought of as a series of curvilinear tracks separated by sharp bends or hairpins. Each loop has a duration of 250 Ma or more. The true situation is no doubt much more complex. These apparently simple tracks will probably be found eventually to be much more irregular than they appear at present and in this paper we present results which indi- cate that between about 1500 and 1250 Ma subordinate loops are present. Geology of the Harp Lake Complex The Harp Lake Complex is an Elsonian pluton lying for the most part within the Western Nain Subprovince of Stockwell (1964). Paleomagnetic studies of the Michikamau Intrusion (Murthy et al. 1968; Emslie et al. 1976) have shown that single magnetizations with a westerly direction predominate. Subordinate antiparallel easterly magnetizations are, however, sometimes present. In contrast, in the Harp Lake Complex, easterly and westerly magnetizations occur with roughly equal frequency. Although rocks with single magnetizations do occur, most of the specimens studied contain two antiparallel magnetizations. These magnetiza- tions are referred to as M and H, and are defined on the basis of their coercivities. The M magnetizations have moderate remanent coercive forces generally in the range 100-1000 Oe (7.96 x lo3-79.6 x lo3 A/m)', but sometimes exceed- ing 2000 Oe (159 x lo3 A/m). For the most part they are carried by magnetite, with a subordinate contribution from hematite. The H magnetiza- tions have much higher coercive forces, com- monly exceeding 2000 Oe (159 x lo3 A/m), and are due to hematite. For reasons given later, it was possible at each site to accurately separate only one of the magnetizations present. Five examples illustrating the range of behaviour are now given. uthwest across the Harp Lake Complex (Fig. 2). They are commonly 30-60 m wide, with chilled margins, and are unmetamorphosed. Chemically the rocks are transitional between alkalic and tholeiitic basalt. In this respect they are similar to the Seal Lake lavas and are believed to be more or less contemporaneous (Meyers 1974). There is some field and geochronological evidence for this opinion. Large slabs and blocks of red arkose and pebble conglomerate occur over a wide area in the western part of the Harp Lake Complex (near sites A10 and All, Fig. 2). The rocks are friable and could not have withstood long- distance transport. A thin section of one of the blocks contains subangular to rounded labor- adorite crystal fragments, lithic pebbles of anorthosite, and two small rounded pebbles of fine-grained, oxidized but otherwise fresh diabase petrographically similar to the Harp dikes. If these red sediments are correlative with the Seal Lake Group red beds cropping out about 15 km to the south, and if the diabase pebbles are indeed from the Harp dikes, then the Harp dikes are either older than, or nearly contemporaneous with, Seal Lake Group sedimentation. The difference between the dikes and the complex indicates that the magnetization of the complex predates the intrusion of the Harp dikes at about 1350 Ma. The presence of reversals and the high blocking temperatures and remanent coercive forces in the anorthositic rocks indicate that the magnetization was acquired at the time of initial cooling about 1450 Ma. At the time of initial cooling the complex was buried beneath cover at a depth of 10 km or more (R. F. Emslie, in preparation). The country rocks have broadly similar directions (Fig. 9), but they are not exactly the same, as is required for a successful contact test. We suggest therefore, that the country rocks became magnetized during uplift some considerable time after intrusion of the complex. There are 3 poles from Australia: from the Morowa lavas, 1390 f 140 Ma (Giddings 1975), from the Lunch Creek lopolith, 1498 _+ 70 Ma (Duff and Embleton 1976), and from a set of metadiabase dikes from the Gawler Block (Giddings and Embleton 1976); and there is one pole from Africa, from the Pilansberg dikes, Rb-Sr age 1310 ) 60 Ma, Gough (1956). On the basis of such a scanty and unbalanced record, it is not possible to construct realistic polar wander curves for the other continents in this time interval. Even for the Laurentian Shield where the data base is several times greater than that for any other Precambrian Shield, the polarity of the poles is uncertain-an ambiguity of 180°! Therefore, the relative positions of the major Precambrian Shields during this interval cannot be unequivocally determined paleomagnetically. [Traduit par le journal] Introduction and adamellitic rocks which range from diorite Paleomagnetic studies of Precambrian rocks from North America carried out during the past 15 years, and especially during the past 5 years, have allowed reasonable estimates to be made of the path of polar wander during much of Proterozoic time. This path is the signature of Precambrian continental drift. Although there is plenty of scope for differences of opinion on details, it is now clear that the path consists of a number of loops which may be thought of as a series of curvilinear tracks separated by sharp bends or hairpins. Each loop has a duration of 250 Ma or more. The true situation is no doubt much more complex. These apparently simple tracks will probably be found eventually to be much more irregular than they appear at present and in this paper we present results which indi- cate that between about 1500 and 1250 Ma subordinate loops are present. Geology of the Harp Lake Complex The Harp Lake Complex is an Elsonian pluton lying for the most part within the Western Nain Subprovince of Stockwell (1964). It is one of several large complexes of anorthositic and related rocks lying north of the Grenville Front in central Labrador (Fig. 1). Th

Subordinate antiparallel easterly magnetizations are, however, sometimes present. In contrast, in the Harp Lake Complex, easterly and westerly magnetizations occur with roughly equal frequency. Chemically the rocks are transitional between alkalic and tholeiitic basalt. In this respect they are similar to the Seal Lake lavas and are believed to be more or less contemporaneous (Meyers 1974). There is some field and geochronological evidence for this opinion. Large slabs and blocks of red arkose and pebble conglomerate occur over a wide area in the western part of the Harp Lake Complex (near sites A10 and All, Fig. 2). The rocks are friable and could not have withstood long- distance transport. A thin section of one of the blocks contains subangular to rounded labor- adorite crystal fragments, lithic pebbles of anorthosite, and two small rounded pebbles of fine-grained, oxidized but otherwise fresh diabase petrographically similar to the Harp dikes. If these red sediments are correlative with the Seal Lake Group red beds cropping out about 15 km to the south, and if the diabase pebbles are indeed from the Harp dikes, then the Harp dikes are either older than, or nearly contemporaneous with, Seal Lake Group sedimentation. [Traduit par le journal] Introduction and adamellitic rocks which range from diorite Paleomagnetic studies of Precambrian rocks from North America carried out during the past 15 years, and especially during the past 5 years, have allowed reasonable estimates to be made of the path of polar wander during much of Proterozoic time. This path is the signature of Precambrian continental drift. Although there is plenty of scope for differences of opinion on details, it is now clear that the path consists of a number of loops which may be thought of as a series of curvilinear tracks separated by sharp bends or hairpins. Each loop has a duration of 250 Ma or more. The true situation is no doubt much more complex. These apparently simple tracks will probably be found eventually to be much more irregular than they appear at present and in this paper we present results which indi- cate that between about 1500 and 1250 Ma subordinate loops are present. Geology of the Harp Lake Complex The Harp Lake Complex is an Elsonian pluton lying for the most part within the Western Nain Subprovince of Stockwell (1964). It is one of several large complexes of anorthositic and related rocks lying north of the Grenville Front in central Labrador (Fig. 1). Th

Usually 5 cores were obtained at each site, and from most cores two cylindrical specimens were cut. The magnet- ization was measured by Schonstedt SMI and DSM magnetometers. Paleomagnetic studies of the Michikamau Intrusion (Murthy et al. 1968; Emslie et al. 1976) have shown that single magnetizations with a westerly direction predominate. Subordinate antiparallel easterly magnetizations are, however, sometimes present. In contrast, in the Harp Lake Complex, easterly and westerly magnetizations occur with roughly equal frequency. Although rocks with single magnetizations do occur, most of the specimens studied contain two antiparallel magnetizations. These magnetiza- tions are referred to as M and H, and are defined on the basis of their coercivities. The M magnetizations have moderate remanent coercive forces generally in the range 100-1000 Oe (7.96 x lo3-79.6 x lo3 A/m)', but sometimes exceed- ing 2000 Oe (159 x lo3 A/m). For the most part they are carried by magnetite, with a subordinate contribution from hematite. The H magnetiza- tions have much higher coercive forces, com- monly exceeding 2000 Oe (159 x lo3 A/m), and are due to hematite. For reasons given later, it was possible at each site to accurately separate only one of the magnetizations present. Five examples illustrating the range of behaviour are now given. The first cycle began with the deposition on Archean terrain of the sandstones and dolomites of the Seward Subgroup. These were collected at eight sites from mainly fine- and medium-grained red arkoses (Fig. 2). The Sokoman Iron Formation, which was deposited near the beginning of the second cycle, was sampled at four sites (Fig. 2). The immediately overlying Menihek Formation (in the western Trough) was sampled from six sites of very fine- grained, maroon to almost black, argillaceous rocks (Fig. 2). A possible third cycle ended with the extrusion of the Willbob basalt. Trough can be divided into two and possibly three tectonic cycles (Fahrig 1957; Dimroth 19683; Dimroth et al. 1970), each of which began with the deposition of orthoquartzites and chemical sediments (e.g. Seward, Sokoman) and ended with the deposition of shales and quartz- ites (e.g. Menihek) in the miogeosyncline, and volcanics (e.g. Willbob, Wakuach, Retty) in the eugeosyncline (Fig. 1). The three cycles are 'Contribution from Earth Physics Branch No. 644. defined by the rock units Seward to Attika- magen, Wishart to Murdoch, and Thompson to Retty (Table 1). The first cycle began with the deposition on Archean terrain of the sandstones and dolomites of the Seward Subgroup. These were collected at eight sites from mainly fine- and medium-grained red arkoses (Fig. 2). The Sokoman Iron Formation, which was deposited near the beginning of the second cycle, was sampled at four sites (Fig. 2). The immediately overlying Menihek Formation (in the western Trough) was sampled from six sites of very fine- grained, maroon to almost black, argillaceous rocks (Fig. 2). A possible third cycle ended with the extrusion of the Willbob basalt. The Wakuach gabbro and Retty peridotite are probably in large part equivalent to the Willbob, but may include sills equivalent to the M

The present paleo- magnetic study is the result of a reconnaissance survey carried out in the centra

Trough can be divided into two and possibly three tectonic cycles (Fahrig 1957; Dimroth 19683; Dimroth et al. 1970), each of which began with the deposition of orthoquartzites and chemical sediments (e.g. Seward, Sokoman) and ended with the deposition of shales and quartz- ites (e.g. Menihek) in the miogeosyncline, and volcanics (e.g. Willbob, Wakuach, Retty) in the eugeosyncline (Fig. 1). The three cycles are 'Contribution from Earth Physics Branch No. 644. defined by the rock units Seward to Attika- magen, Wishart to Murdoch, and Thompson to Retty (Table 1). The first cycle began with the deposition on Archean terrain of the sandstones and dolomites of the Seward Subgroup. These were collected at eight sites from mainly fine- and medium-grained red arkoses (Fig. 2). The Sokoman Iron Formation, which was deposited near the beginning of the second cycle, was sampled at four sites (Fig. 2). The immediately overlying Menihek Formation (in the western Trough) was sampled from six sites of very fine- grained, maroon to almost black, argillaceous rocks (Fig. 2). A possible third cycle ended with the extrusion of the Willbob basalt. The Wakuach gabbro and Retty peridotite are probably in large part equivalent to the Willbob, but may include sills equivalent to the M

The present paleo- magnetic study is the result of a reconnaissance survey carried out in the centra

Trough can be divided into two and possibly three tectonic cycles (Fahrig 1957; Dimroth 19683; Dimroth et al. 1970), each of which began with the deposition of orthoquartzites and chemical sediments (e.g. Seward, Sokoman) and ended with the deposition of shales and quartz- ites (e.g. Menihek) in the miogeosyncline, and volcanics (e.g. Willbob, Wakuach, Retty) in the eugeosyncline (Fig. 1). The three cycles are 'Contribution from Earth Physics Branch No. 644. defined by the rock units Seward to Attika- magen, Wishart to Murdoch, and Thompson to Retty (Table 1). The first cycle began with the deposition on Archean terrain of the sandstones and dolomites of the Seward Subgroup. These were collected at eight sites from mainly fine- and medium-grained red arkoses (Fig. 2). The Sokoman Iron Formation, which was deposited near the beginning of the second cycle, was sampled at four sites (Fig. 2). The immediately overlying Menihek Formation (in the western Trough) was sampled from six sites of very fine- grained, maroon to almost black, argillaceous rocks (Fig. 2). A possible third cycle ended with the extrusion of the Willbob basalt. The Wakuach gabbro and Retty peridotite are probably in large part equivalent to the Willbob, but may include sills equivalent to the M

The Sokoman Iron Formation, which was deposited near the beginning of the second cycle, was sampled at four sites (Fig. 2). A possible third cycle ended with the extrusion of the Willbob basalt. The Wakuach gabbro and Retty peridotite are probably in large part equivalent to the Willbob, but may include sills equivalent to the Menihek and earlier volcanics. Samples were collected from 11 sites in the Willbob, 9 in the Wakuach, and 3 in the Retty (Fig. 2). Rocks from the Flin Flon area may be related to this zone, and it is noteworthy that they exhibit two magnetizations that show certain similarities to the Labrador Trough magnetizations. The dominant magnetization at Flin Flon, which is probably largely the result of cooling following uplift, has poles that agree very closely with the SB, MB, and RB poles from the Labrador Trough. At Flin Flon, a subordinate but more stable magnetization, which is thought to be a primary t in the ultrabasic Boundary Intrusions (dated 7 a about 1800 Ma), has a pole near to the A poles from the Trough. Trough can be divided into two and possibly three tectonic cycles (Fahrig 1957; Dimroth 19683; Dimroth et al. 1970), each of which began with the deposition of orthoquartzites and chemical sediments (e.g. Seward, Sokoman) and ended with the deposition of shales and quartz- ites (e.g. Menihek) in the miogeosyncline, and volcanics (e.g. Willbob, Wakuach, Retty) in the eugeosyncline (Fig. 1). The three cycles are 'Contribution from Earth Physics Branch No. 644. defined by the rock units Seward to Attika- magen, Wishart to Murdoch, and Thompson to Retty (Table 1). The first cycle began with the deposition on Archean terrain of the sandstones and dolomites of the Seward Subgroup. These were collected at eight sites from mainly fine- and medium-grained red arkoses (Fig. 2). The Sokoman Iron Formation, which was deposited near the beginning of the second cycle, was sampled at four sites (Fig. 2). The immediately overlying Menihek Formation (in the western Trough) was sampled from six sites of very fine- grained, maroon to almost black, argillaceous rocks (Fig. 2). A possible third cycle ended with the extrusion of the Willbob basalt. The Sokoman Iron Formation, which was deposited near the beginning of the second cycle, was sampled at four sites (Fig. 2). A possible third cycle ended with the extrusion of the Willbob basalt. The magnetizations are complex. Most magnetizations are secondary and none are demonstrably original, but their relative order can be estimated from their associated hlocking temperatures. The oldest magnetizations (A) are thought to have been acquired at about 1800 Ma following deposition but not necessarily long afterwards. These magnetizations have blocking temperatures of about 600 "C and occur in the Seward Subgroup [mainly arkoses), the Menihek Formation (arpillites), and the Retty Formation (peridotites). The Castignon carbonatitic complex also has A type magnetizations which are referred. tentatively, to a K-Ar date of 1875 k 50 Ma. The next youngest rnagnetizations (B) have blocking ternpera- tures commonly distributed between 300 and 500 "C and are considered to have been acquired at about 1600 Ma during uplift following the Hudsonian orogeny. The Circum-Ungava belt may have been continuous with other supracrustal rock se- quences near the boundary of the Superior and Churchill Structural Provinces in Manitoba (McGlynn 1970). Rocks from the Flin Flon area may be related to this zone, and it is noteworthy that they exhibit two magnetizations that show certain similarities to the Labrador Trough magnetizations. The dominant magnetization at Flin Flon, which is probably largely the result of cooling following uplift, has poles that agree very closely with the SB, MB, and RB poles from the Labrador Trough. At Flin Flon, a subordinate but more stable magnetization, which is thought to be a primary t in the ultrabasic Boundary Intrusions (dated 7 a about 1800 Ma), has a pole near to the A poles from the Trough. Thus the early and later magnetizations at Flin Flon appear to have their correlatives in the Labrador Trough, indicating that the later thermal histories of both areas are broadly similar. The three cycles are 'Contribution from Earth Physics Branch No. 644. defined by the rock units Seward to Attika- magen, Wishart to Murdoch, and Thompson to Retty (Table 1). The first cycle began with the deposition on Archean terrain of the sandstones and dolomites of the Seward Subgroup. These were collected at eight sites from mainly fine- and medium-grained red arkoses (Fig. 2). The Sokoman Iron Formation, which was deposited near the beginning of the second cycle, was sampled at four sites (Fig. 2). The immediately overlying Menihek Formation (in the western Trough) was sampled from six sites of very fine- grained, maroon to almost black, argillaceous rocks (Fig. 2). The magnetizations are complex. Most magnetizations are secondary and none are demonstrably original, but their relative order can be estimated from their associated hlocking temperatures. The oldest magnetizations (A) are thought to have been acquired at about 1800 Ma following deposition but not necessarily long afterwards. These magnetizations have blocking temperatures of about 600 "C and occur in the Seward Subgroup [mainly arkoses), the Menihek Formation (arpillites), and the Retty Formation (peridotites). The Castignon carbonatitic complex also has A type magnetizations which are referred. tentatively, to a K-Ar date of 1875 k 50 Ma. Earth Sci., 14, 159-174 (1977) Geology and Geochronology The Labrador Trough, together with the Cape Smith Belt and the Belcher Islands Belt, is an erosional remnant of a possibly once continuous belt of Aphebian rocks called the Circum- Ungava Geosyncline (Fig. 1). The present paleo- magnetic study is the result of a reconnaissance survey carried out in the centra

Trough can be divided into two and possibly three tectonic cycles (Fahrig 1957; Dimroth 19683; Dimroth et al. 1970), each of which began with the deposition of orthoquartzites and chemical sediments (e.g. Seward, Sokoman) and ended with the deposition of shales and quartz- ites (e.g. Menihek) in the miogeosyncline, and volcanics (e.g. Willbob, Wakuach, Retty) in the eugeosyncline (Fig. 1). The three cycles are 'Contribution from Earth Physics Branch No. 644. defined by the rock units Seward to Attika- magen, Wishart to Murdoch, and Thompson to Retty (Table 1). The first cycle began with the deposition on Archean terrain of the sandstones and dolomites of the Seward Subgroup. These were collected at eight sites from mainly fine- and medium-grained red arkoses (Fig. 2). The Sokoman Iron Formation, which was deposited near the beginning of the second cycle, was sampled at four sites (Fig. 2). The immediately overlying Menihek Formation (in the western Trough) was sampled from six sites of very fine- grained, maroon to almost black, argillaceous rocks (Fig. 2). A possible third cycle ended with the extrusion of the Willbob basalt. The Wakuach gabbro and Retty peridotite are probably in large part equivalent to the Willbob, but may include sills equivalent to the M

A possible third cycle ended with the extrusion of the Willbob basalt. The Wakuach gabbro and Retty peridotite are probably in large part equivalent to the Willbob, but may include sills equivalent to the Menihek and earlier volcanics. Samples were collected from 11 sites in the Willbob, 9 in the Wakuach, and 3 in the Retty (Fig. 2). The magnetizations are complex. Most magnetizations are secondary and none are demonstrably original, but their relative order can be estimated from their associated hlocking temperatures. The oldest magnetizations (A) are thought to have been acquired at about 1800 Ma following deposition but not necessarily long afterwards. These magnetizations have blocking temperatures of about 600 "C and occur in the Seward Subgroup [mainly arkoses), the Menihek Formation (arpillites), and the Retty Formation (peridotites). The Castignon carbonatitic complex also has A type magnetizations which are referred. tentatively, to a K-Ar date of 1875 k 50 Ma. Earth Sci., 14, 159-174 (1977) Geology and Geochronology The Labrador Trough, together with the Cape Smith Belt and the Belcher Islands Belt, is an erosional remnant of a possibly once continuous belt of Aphebian rocks called the Circum- Ungava Geosyncline (Fig. 1). The present paleo- magnetic study is the result of a reconnaissance survey carried out in the centra

Trough can be divided into two and possibly three tectonic cycles (Fahrig 1957; Dimroth 19683; Dimroth et al. 1970), each of which began with the deposition of orthoquartzites and chemical sediments (e.g. Seward, Sokoman) and ended with the deposition of shales and quartz- ites (e.g. Menihek) in the miogeosyncline, and volcanics (e.g. Willbob, Wakuach, Retty) in the eugeosyncline (Fig. 1). The three cycles are 'Contribution from Earth Physics Branch No. 644. defined by the rock units Seward to Attika- magen, Wishart to Murdoch, and Thompson to Retty (Table 1). The first cycle began with the deposition on Archean terrain of the sandstones and dolomites of the Seward Subgroup. These were collected at eight sites from mainly fine- and medium-grained red arkoses (Fig. 2). The Sokoman Iron Formation, which was deposited near the beginning of the second cycle, was sampled at four sites (Fig. 2). The immediately overlying Menihek Formation (in the western Trough) was sampled from six sites of very fine- grained, maroon to almost black, argillaceous rocks (Fig. 2). A possible third cycle ended with the extrusion of the Willbob basalt. The Wakuach gabbro and Retty peridotite are probably in large part equivalent to the Willbob, but may include sills equivalent to the M

The three cycles are 'Contribution from Earth Physics Branch No. 644. defined by the rock units Seward to Attika- magen, Wishart to Murdoch, and Thompson to Retty (Table 1). The first cycle began with the deposition on Archean terrain of the sandstones and dolomites of the Seward Subgroup. These were collected at eight sites from mainly fine- and medium-grained red arkoses (Fig. 2). The Sokoman Iron Formation, which was deposited near the beginning of the second cycle, was sampled at four sites (Fig. 2). The immediately overlying Menihek Formation (in the western Trough) was sampled from six sites of very fine- grained, maroon to almost black, argillaceous rocks (Fig. 2). A possible third cycle ended with the extrusion of the Willbob basalt. The sites represent the Ponder, Alastair Lake, and Quottoon plutons in the 40-50 Ma eastern K-Ar age zone and the Ecstall and Butedale plutons in the 64-80 Ma central age zone. After af demagnetization a stable remanent magnetization was isolated at 32 sites and these data were combined with available data from the Skeena River section about 100 km to the north. The remanence directions in sites from the NNW-trending north and south limbs of the Hawkesbury Warp provide a positive fold test when compared to the WNW-trending centre limh directions. In the Eocene eastern age zone the NNW limbs give a concordant pole position relative to the cratonic North American pole whereas the centre limb has undergone 90" of the counter- clockwise rotation and =10"of upward tilt of its western end topive H discoldant pole. Earth Sci., 14, 1246-1262 (1977) Introduction The age of emplacement of the plutonic rocks that form the Coast plutonic complex remains a major uncertainty in the interpretation of Cordilleran geology. Geologic field relations place their time of intrustion between Late Jurassic and Late Miocene. Hutchison (1967, 1970) and Monger and Hutchison (1971) noted that the K-Ar radiometric ages from plutons along the length of the complex form an eastern zone of 40-50 Ma, a central zone of 64-80 Ma, and a western

overlying Lower Creta- ceous sediments. Hutchison (1970) has summarized the pe- trology and structure of the central Coast plutonic complex. lndividual plutons are elon- gate, often tadpole-shaped, and they parallel the NNW trend of the complex. They may exceed 100 km in length as does the Quottoon pluton, or 30 km in width as do the Ponder and Butedale plutons. The plutons generally have a perimeter phase of foliated or gneissic diorite with minor gabbroic zones. Progressing towards their core they become increasingly massive and grade from quartz diorite, to granodiorite, to a massive quartz monzonite core. The Ponder, Alastair Lake, and Quottoon plutons lie in the eastern age zone. The Ponder pluton gives K-Ar ages on biotite of 46 f 10 and 47 +4 Ma (GSC 65-32 and 66-15 in Wanless et al. (1967, 1968)). The Alastair Lake pluton gives a biotite K-Ar age of 44 f 4 Ma (GSC 65-30). It appears to be the southward equivalent of the Kasiks pluton which was previously sampled (Symons 1974a) and gives a biotite K-Ar age of 43 f 5 Ma (GSC 65-29). The Quottoon pluton gives biotite and hornblende K-Ar ages of 44 + 5, 48 + 9, 49 +4, 49 + 7, and 50 f 5 Ma (GSC 66-6, 7, 8, and 9; and GSC 67-25 in Wanless et al. Earth Sci., 14, 1246-1262 (1977) Introduction The age of emplacement of the plutonic rocks that form the Coast plutonic complex remains a major uncertainty in the interpretation of Cordilleran geology. Geologic field relations place their time of intrustion between Late Jurassic and Late Miocene. Hutchison (1967, 1970) and Monger and Hutchison (1971) noted that the K-Ar radiometric ages from plutons along the length of the complex form an eastern zone of 40-50 Ma, a central zone of 64-80 Ma, and a western

overlying Lower Creta- ceous sediments. Hutchison (1970) has summarized the pe- trology and structure of the central Coast plutonic complex. lndividual plutons are elon- gate, often tadpole-shaped, and they parallel the NNW trend of the complex. They may exceed 100 km in length as does the Quottoon pluton, or 30 km in width as do the Ponder and Butedale plutons. The plutons generally have a perimeter phase of foliated or gneissic diorite with minor gabbroic zones. Progressing towards their core they become increasingly massive and grade from quartz diorite, to granodiorite, to a massive quartz monzonite core. The Ponder, Alastair Lake, and Quottoon plutons lie in the eastern age zone. The Ponder pluton gives K-Ar ages on biotite of 46 f 10 and 47 +4 Ma (GSC 65-32 and 66-15 in Wanless et al. (1967, 1968)). The Alastair Lake pluton gives a biotite K-Ar age of 44 f 4 Ma (GSC 65-30). It appears to be the southward equivalent of the Kasiks pluton which was previously sampled (Symons 1974a) and gives a biotite K-Ar age of 43 f 5 Ma (GSC 65-29). Eslinger and Savin (1973) have surmised, from 180/160 ratios of coexisting quartz and illite, that isotopic temperatures ranged from 225 "C to 310 "C in the Lower Belt Supergroup during the event. Elimination of the Eocambrian magnetization occurred mostly between 300" and 550 "C (Fig. 4) but sometimes even higher; using theoretical relationships between blocking temperatures and relaxation time calculated by Dunlop (in Pullaiah et al. 1975) it is estimated that a range of temperatures between 100" and 300 "C could indeed have been responsible for the Eocambrian magnetization, if hematite is the carrier of the magnetization. Hematite appears to be the most likely mineral; ferrous-ferric ratios for the Spokane argillites are very low (Ross 1959, p. 55). The small amount of ferrous iron can be totally accounted for by iron as octahedral cations in illite (Maxwell and Hower 1967, p. 850) or in carbonate minerals, making the presence of more than trace amounts of magnetite quite unlikely. Temperatures of much more than about 200 "C are generally inconsistent with the low meta- morphic grade of the argillites, and the lower limit of the inferred isotopic and magnetic temperatures is favored at present. Conclusions The Spokane Formation has yielded a geo- magnetic pole position, based on high-tempera- ture magnetizations, that agrees well with contemporaneous Helikian (' Elsonian ') poles from different parts of the North American craton. In addition these sediments recorded a Late Hadrynian magnetization that appears to be associated with low-grade metamorphism chang- ing the claystones to argillites. The Helikian magnetization residing in fine-grained hematite has survived this remagnetization. produced the Eocambrian partial remagnetization. Eslinger and Savin (1973) have surmised, from 180/160 ratios of coexisting quartz and illite, that isotopic temperatures ranged from 225 "C to 310 "C in the Lower Belt Supergroup during the event. Elimination of the Eocambrian magnetization occurred mostly between 300" and 550 "C (Fig. 4) but sometimes even higher; using theoretical relationships between blocking temperatures and relaxation time calculated by Dunlop (in Pullaiah et al. 1975) it is estimated that a range of temperatures between 100" and 300 "C could indeed have been responsible for the Eocambrian magnetization, if hematite is the carrier of the magnetization. Hematite appears to be the most likely mineral; ferrous-ferric ratios for the Spokane argillites are very low (Ross 1959, p. 55). The small amount of ferrous iron can be totally accounted for by iron as octahedral cations in illite (Maxwell and Hower 1967, p. 850) or in carbonate minerals, making the presence of more than trace amounts of magnetite quite unlikely. Temperatures of much more than about 200 "C are generally inconsistent with the low meta- morphic grade of the argillites, and the lower limit of the inferred isotopic and magnetic temperatures is favored at present. Conclusions The Spokane Formation has yielded a geo- magnetic pole position, based on high-tempera- ture magnetizations, that agrees well with contemporaneous Helikian (' Elsonian ') poles from different parts of the North American craton. x and Doell (1960) calculated a pole position of 168"E, 1"s using the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) direc- tions of 58 specimens from the remaining 9 sam- ples. This result has been often disregarded be- cause of the lack of AF cleaning on all specimens. Nevertheless the Umfraville gabbro is one of the most likely units in the Grenville Province to have retained a primary thermoremanent magnetization (TRM), which bears directly on arguments con- cerning the possible translation or rotation of the Grenville orogen relative to the rest of the Canadian Precambrian Shield. Geology The Umfraville gabbro was first mapped by Adams and Barlow (1910) on a regional scale. Re- cently it has been mapped at 1 in. : d mile as part of four map-areas by Hewitt and James (1956), Hewitt (1959, 1962), and Lumbers (1969). The host rocks in the Hastings Basin for the ! Umfraville gabbro are strata of the Hermon and Mayo Groups (Lumbers 1967) (Fig. 1) that have 1 been regionally metamorphosed to greenschist and amphibolite facies. The sequence grades from the basal mafic metavolcanics of the Tudor formation ' (lower Hermon Group), upwards through felsic , metavolcanics of the Oak Lake formation (middle I Hermon Group), through clastic siliceous metased- iments of the Van

The units in order of decreasing age are: the Hermon and Mayo metavolcanics and metasediments (no pattern); the sodic intrusive trondhjemite (crossed lines); the Umfraville gabbro and related stocks (diagonal lines); and the late potassic syenite (stipple). Silver from the syenite phase (S. B. Lumbers, per- sonal communication, 1978). The massive Um- fraville gabbro is about 10 km long by 4 km wide. It has minor zones of olivine gabbro, anorthositic gabbro, and diorite. Late phases of potassic syenite and pyroxenitic monzonite occur around its perimeter and in minor cross-cutting dikes. Titanomagnetite is the only significant magnetic mineral and it results in a 4000nT1 positive aeromagnetic anomaly (GSC 1959). Ifpresent, reg- ional metamorphism of the Umfraville gabbro has not reached the greenschist facies. Other stocks in the group show local alteration of their primary pyroxene and plagioclase by autometamorphism. Earth Sci., 15,936-962 (1978) Introduction The Umfraville gabbro is located about 20 km south of Bancroft, Ontario, in the Hastings Basin of the Grenville Province. Hood (1958) selected the gabbro for one of the earliest paleomagnetic studies in Canada because it is virtually unmetamor- phosed. The use of alternating field (AF) demag- netization was just being developed at that time. Hood (1958) did an AF cleaning test on one speci- men from each of 12 hand samples collected from along the old Hastings Road (Fig. I), and rejected 3 samples as magnetically unstable. Cox and Doell (1960) calculated a pole position of 168"E, 1"s using the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) direc- tions of 58 specimens from the remaining 9 sam- ples. This result has been often disregarded be- cause of the lack of AF cleaning on all specimens. Nevertheless the Umfraville gabbro is one of the most likely units in the Grenville Province to have retained a primary thermoremanent magnetization (TRM), which bears directly on arguments con- cerning the possible translation or rotation of the Grenville orogen relat

g the possible translation or rotation of the Grenville orogen relative to the rest of the Canadian Precambrian Shield. Geology The Umfraville gabbro was first mapped by Adams and Barlow (1910) on a regional scale. Re- cently it has been mapped at 1 in. : d mile as part of four map-areas by Hewitt and James (1956), Hewitt (1959, 1962), and Lumbers (1969). The host rocks in the Hastings Basin for the ! Umfraville gabbro are strata of the Hermon and Mayo Groups (Lumbers 1967) (Fig. 1) that have 1 been regionally metamorphosed to greenschist and amphibolite facies. The sequence grades from the basal mafic metavolcanics of the Tudor formation ' (lower Hermon Group), upwards through felsic , metavolcanics of the Oak Lake formation (middle I Hermon Group), through clastic siliceous metased- iments of the Vansickle formation (upper Hermon Group), which include the Turriff metavolcanic sequence, to the uppermost carbonate meta- sedimentary strata of the Dungannon formation (Mayo Group), which also includes the Burnt Lake metavolcanic sequence. The basal Tudor metavol- canics were extruded about 1310 k 15 Ma ago based on U-Pb radiometric ages for zircons from two metarhyolite specimens (Silver and Lumbers 1966). ions of the deposits of the Coronation Geos yncline and associated aulacogen. These deposits record the phases of a classical geosynclinal cycle for which Hoffman has provided a beautiful interpretation in terms of an ocean-con- tinent plate interaction (Hoffman 1973). The Coro- nation loop appears, in part at least, to be the paleomagnetic signature of this cycle. The rate of motion relative to the pole, that is the rate of change of latitude, is about 5 cm year-'. The major defor- mation phase occurs during and after the deposi- tion of the Great Slave Supergroup, but before the deposition of the Et-Then Group, so the bend or hairpin of the Coronation loop corresponds to that deformational phase. During this deformational phase, the Coronation Geosyncline was in latitudes of about 25" (Seton Formation), moved to equa- torial latitudes (Christie Bay Group) and then back to a latitude of about 25" (Et-Then Group). Thus the major deformation phase of the Coronation Geo- syncline corresponds to a large change in direction of the motions of the Laurentian plate as recorded paleomagnetically between the Pearson and the Et-Then. The orogenic phase of the Coronation Geosyn- cline, which is dated about - 1800 Ma, appears to post-date certain Hudsonian events in th

useful physically recognizable boundary between the Aphebian and Helikian. The type loca- tion is the East Arm of the Great Slave Lake, and the pole change corresponding to the observed magnetic change is as described in Fig. 10. The current best estimate of the time at which this change occurred is - 1800 Ma. The Et-Then Group contains thin basic volcanic members (Hoffman 1968), acd hence, like the Pearson Formation, could possibly be dated, so that in principle the boundary could be more accurately fixed in time. ions of the deposits of the Coronation Geos yncline and associated aulacogen. These deposits record the phases of a classical geosynclinal cycle for which Hoffman has provided a beautiful interpretation in terms of an ocean-con- tinent plate interaction (Hoffman 1973). The Coro- nation loop appears, in part at least, to be the paleomagnetic signature of this cycle. The rate of motion relative to the pole, that is the rate of change of latitude, is about 5 cm year-'. The major defor- mation phase occurs during and after the deposi- tion of the Great Slave Supergroup, but before the deposition of the Et-Then Group, so the bend or hairpin of the Coronation loop corresponds to that deformational phase. During this deformational phase, the Coronation Geosyncline was in latitudes of about 25" (Seton Formation), moved to equa- torial latitudes (Christie Bay Group) and then back to a latitude of about 25" (Et-Then Group). Thus the major deformation phase of the Coronation Geo- syncline corresponds to a large change in direction of the motions of the Laurentian plate as recorded paleomagnetically between the Pearson and the Et-Then. The orogenic phase of the Coronation Geosyn- cline, which is dated about - 1800 Ma, appears to post-date certain Hudsonian events in th

The type loca- tion is the East Arm of the Great Slave Lake, and the pole change corresponding to the observed magnetic change is as described in Fig. 10. The current best estimate of the time at which this change occurred is - 1800 Ma. The Et-Then Group contains thin basic volcanic members (Hoffman 1968), acd hence, like the Pearson Formation, could possibly be dated, so that in principle the boundary could be more accurately fixed in time. ions of the deposits of the Coronation Geos yncline and associated aulacogen. These deposits record the phases of a classical geosynclinal cycle for which Hoffman has provided a beautiful interpretation in terms of an ocean-con- tinent plate interaction (Hoffman 1973). The Coro- nation loop appears, in part at least, to be the paleomagnetic signature of this cycle. The rate of motion relative to the pole, that is the rate of change of latitude, is about 5 cm year-'. The major defor- mation phase occurs during and after the deposi- tion of the Great Slave Supergroup, but before the deposition of the Et-Then Group, so the bend or hairpin of the Coronation loop corresponds to that deformational phase. During this deformational phase, the Coronation Geosyncline was in latitudes of about 25" (Seton Formation), moved to equa- torial latitudes (Christie Bay Group) and then back to a latitude of about 25" (Et-Then Group). Thus the major deformation phase of the Coronation Geo- syncline corresponds to a large change in direction of the motions of the Laurentian plate as recorded paleomagnetically between the Pearson and the Et-Then. The orogenic phase of the Coronation Geosyn- cline, which is dated about - 1800 Ma, appears to post-date certain Hudsonian events in th

useful physically recognizable boundary between the Aphebian and Helikian. The type loca- tion is the East Arm of the Great Slave Lake, and the pole change corresponding to the observed magnetic change is as described in Fig. 10. The current best estimate of the time at which this change occurred is - 1800 Ma. The Et-Then Group contains thin basic volcanic members (Hoffman 1968), acd hence, like the Pearson Formation, could possibly be dated, so that in principle the boundary could be more accurately fixed in time. ions of the deposits of the Coronation Geos yncline and associated aulacogen. These deposits record the phases of a classical geosynclinal cycle for which Hoffman has provided a beautiful interpretation in terms of an ocean-con- tinent plate interaction (Hoffman 1973). The Coro- nation loop appears, in part at least, to be the paleomagnetic signature of this cycle. The rate of motion relative to the pole, that is the rate of change of latitude, is about 5 cm year-'. The major defor- mation phase occurs during and after the deposi- tion of the Great Slave Supergroup, but before the deposition of the Et-Then Group, so the bend or hairpin of the Coronation loop corresponds to that deformational phase. During this deformational phase, the Coronation Geosyncline was in latitudes of about 25" (Seton Formation), moved to equa- torial latitudes (Christie Bay Group) and then back to a latitude of about 25" (Et-Then Group). Thus the major deformation phase of the Coronation Geo- syncline corresponds to a large change in direction of the motions of the Laurentian plate as recorded paleomagnetically between the Pearson and the Et-Then. The orogenic phase of the Coronation Geosyn- cline, which is dated about - 1800 Ma, appears to post-date certain Hudsonian events in th

useful physically recognizable boundary between the Aphebian and Helikian. The type loca- tion is the East Arm of the Great Slave Lake, and the pole change corresponding to the observed magnetic change is as described in Fig. 10. The current best estimate of the time at which this change occurred is - 1800 Ma. The Et-Then Group contains thin basic volcanic members (Hoffman 1968), acd hence, like the Pearson Formation, could possibly be dated, so that in principle the boundary could be more accurately fixed in time. s province. This paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of the lower two-thirds of the lava stratigraphy comprising three groups of flows separated by sediments. The lower group (palaeomagnetic pole at 239°E, 7°N, 7 sites, dq~ = 7.6 ° , d× = 14.1 °) includes one reversal of magnetisa- tion and two intermediate directions, and the upper group (pole at 222°E, 16°N, 24 sites, dq, = 4.8 ° , d× = 9.0 °) in- cludes four reversals and two intermediate directions. The middle group of 13 lavas yields anomalous directions with respect to the other groups and appears to have been erupted during a polarity excursion of uncertain significance. Opaque petrographic analysis reveals all stages of deuteric oxidation (800-500°C) plus lower-temperature hydro- thermal alteration to epidote grade. In addition to high reversal frequency, the succession illustrates asymmetry of the dipole source, and there is a suggestion that lavas with easterly directed magnetisations have higher deuteric oxidation states than those with westerly directed magnetisations. Collective palaeomagnetic results from the Gardar Province are linked to a number of Rb-Sr isochrons, and com- parison with contemporaneous North American data confirms the 500-fathom continental reconstruction for Proterozoic times. Ade-Hall et al [11] regard hemati- sation of magnetite and relict ilmenite in a base of titanohematite and ferri-rutile as diagnostic of hydro- thermal alteration of class 3 and 4 grains in the epidote (1) zone. Hematisation is widely developed in this col- lection, notably in the middle group (Table 2), al- though since it is very finely divided the precise amount is difficult to measure. It is apparently un- related to deuteric oxidation because samples with both low and high deuteric oxidation states are af- fected to comparable degrees; it is ubiquitous where the primary magnetite grain size is smallest (Table 2). This effect is therefore attributable to regional hydro- thermal alteration and its significance in the context of remagnetisation is discussed in section 7. 5. Thermomagnetic characteristics Keweenawan lavas from the epidote zone are characterised by distinctive thermomagnetic curves [11 ] with a (as yet unexplained) rise in saturation magnetisation (Js)between 100 and 200°C to produce a kink (Fig. 3), and an irreversible inflection ("e" point) between 300 and 450°C. This collection is more varied and inflection points and kinks are con- fined to a few lavas mostly in the upper group (Table 1).

Ade-Hall et al [11] regard hemati- sation of magnetite and relict ilmenite in a base of titanohematite and ferri-rutile as diagnostic of hydro- thermal alteration of class 3 and 4 grains in the epidote (1) zone. Hematisation is widely developed in this col- lection, notably in the middle group (Table 2), al- though since it is very finely divided the precise amount is difficult to measure. It is apparently un- related to deuteric oxidation because samples with both low and high deuteric oxidation states are af- fected to comparable degrees; it is ubiquitous where the primary magnetite grain size is smallest (Table 2). This effect is therefore attributable to regional hydro- thermal alteration and its significance in the context of remagnetisation is discussed in section 7. 5. Thermomagnetic characteristics Keweenawan lavas from the epidote zone are characterised by distinctive thermomagnetic curves [11 ] with a (as yet unexplained) rise in saturation magnetisation (Js)between 100 and 200°C to produce a kink (Fig. 3), and an irreversible inflection ("e" point) between 300 and 450°C. This collection is more varied and inflection points and kinks are con- fined to a few lavas mostly in the upper group (Table 1).

Introduction The Proterozoic Gardar igneous cycle of South Greenland [1 ] commenced with eruption of basaltic lavas and deposition of continental sandstones (Eriksfjord Formation), nearly contemporary with, or followed by, intrusion of major alkaline igneous bodies, syenite and gabbro giant dykes and a whole range of acid to basic minor intrusions. The lavas within the Eriksfjord Formation have an aggregate thickness of over 1500 m [2] ; not only are they well exposed, but intervening clastic horizons show that the extrusion of the earlier phases spanned a con- siderable period of time. s province. This paper reports a palaeomagnetic study of the lower two-thirds of the lava stratigraphy comprising three groups of flows separated by sediments. The lower group (palaeomagnetic pole at 239°E, 7°N, 7 sites, dq~ = 7.6 ° , d× = 14.1 °) includes one reversal of magnetisa- tion and two intermediate directions, and the upper group (pole at 222°E, 16°N, 24 sites, dq, = 4.8 ° , d× = 9.0 °) in- cludes four reversals and two intermediate directions. The middle group of 13 lavas yields anomalous directions with respect to the other groups and appears to have been erupted during a polarity excursion of uncertain significance. Opaque petrographic analysis reveals all stages of deuteric oxidation (800-500°C) plus lower-temperature hydro- thermal alteration to epidote grade. In addition to high reversal frequency, the succession illustrates asymmetry of the dipole source, and there is a suggestion that lavas with easterly directed magnetisations have higher deuteric oxidation states than those with westerly directed magnetisations. Collective palaeomagnetic results from the Gardar Province are linked to a number of Rb-Sr isochrons, and com- parison with contemporaneous North American data confirms the 500-fathom continental reconstruction for Proterozoic times. In the laboratory the cores were sliced into 2.5-cm cylinders and measured before and after progressive alternating field (a.f.) demagnetisation using a para- static magnetometer; the step-wise a.f. cleaning was normally undertaken in steps of 50 oersteds (Oe) up to maximum peak fields between 500 and 1400 Oe. The salient petrologic properties are listed in Table 2 where it is clear that several characteristics are typical of the deuteric alteration observed in Ter- tiary and Recent lavas. Firstly, 58% of thiscollection have oxidation numbers higher than 3. Ade-Hall et al [11] regard hemati- sation of magnetite and relict ilmenite in a base of titanohematite and ferri-rutile as diagnostic of hydro- thermal alteration of class 3 and 4 grains in the epidote (1) zone. Hematisation is widely developed in this col- lection, notably in the middle group (Table 2), al- though since it is very finely divided the precise amount is difficult to measure. It is apparently un- related to deuteric oxidation because samples with both low and high deuteric oxidation states are af- fected to comparable degrees; it is ubiquitous where the primary magnetite grain size is smallest (Table 2). This effect is therefore attributable to regional hydro- thermal alteration and its significance in the context of remagnetisation is discussed in section 7. 5. Thermomagnetic characteristics Keweenawan lavas from the epidote zone are characterised by distinctive thermomagnetic curves [11 ] with a (as yet unexplained) rise in saturation magnetisation (Js)between 100 and 200°C to produce a kink (Fig. 3), and an irreversible inflection ("e" point) between 300 and 450°C. This collection is more varied and inflection points and kinks are con- fined to a few lavas mostly in the upper group (Table 1).

Introduction The Proterozoic Gardar igneous cycle of South Greenland [1 ] commenced with eruption of basaltic lavas and deposition of continental sandstones (Eriksfjord Formation), nearly contemporary with, or followed by, intrusion of major alkaline igneous bodies, syenite and gabbro giant dykes and a whole range of acid to basic minor intrusions. The lavas within the Eriksfjord Formation have an aggregate thickness of over 1500 m [2] ; not only are they well exposed, but intervening clastic horizons show that the extrusion of the earlier phases spanned a con- siderable period of time. The lavas within the Eriksfjord Formation have an aggregate thickness of over 1500 m [2] ; not only are they well exposed, but intervening clastic horizons show that the extrusion of the earlier phases spanned a con- siderable period of time. The latter are both less than 150 km from Kimberley and al- though undated are geologically correlated with the Kimberley pipes. Eighty blocks, oriented without recourse to magnetic methods, have been collected from the five pipes. The samples comprise kimberlite, accidental inclusions of widely varying lithologies and wall rock thus enabling inclusion and baked contact tests to be performed. Extensive alternating field and thermal demagnetization experiments show that the magnetization of the kimberlite is primary. Secular variation is not averaged out in any one pipe (with the possible exception of Finsch) and it is suggested the three Kimberley pipes were emplaced simultaneously. The mean pole position of the five pipes (57.2 ° E, 58.2°S with K = 25.8 and A95 = 15.3 °) is believed to be a good estimate of the palaeomagnetic pole 86 -+ 3 Ma ago. The reliability of the pole is ascertained through thermal demagnetization, a fold test, comparison between red beds and a lava flow, and the presence of normal and reversed polarities. The Timor pole is in excellent agreement with the Australian Upper Permian and Triassic poles. From this it is inferred that autochthonous Timor formed part of the Australian continental margin at least since the Upper Permian. 1.
